1. Executive Summary
VIT Code Apex 3.0 was organized by the Artificial Intelligence Students’ Forum (AISF) at Vishwakarma Institute of Technology  
(VIT), Pune. The event brought student teams together to develop technology-driven responses to practical and industry-relevant  
challenges. Its hybrid structure combined online screening and an online jury-pitch round with a 24-hour on-campus Grand Finale  
at VIT Bibwewadi Campus.
The  event  attracted  800+  registered  teams  representing  125  colleges.  After  the  first-round  screening,  532  teams  advanced. 
Following the second-round online jury pitches, 104 teams were selected for the Grand Finale. The on-campus hackathon began at  
11:00 AM and continued for 24 hours, with continuous evaluation reported during the finale.
Four tracks gave participants different routes into the competition: Emerson, iMocha, Open Innovation, and Technology for Social  
Impact powered by UST. The challenge themes ranged from AI-supported industrial diagram conversion and control-cabinet  
inspection to software quality assurance, skills evidence, workplace simulations, open problem-solving, cold-storage excursion  
warnings, indoor positioning, and sensor reliability.
The overall winners were Kala Dhua (first place), The Sapiens (second place), and Astranyx (third place). Their cash awards were  
50,000, 30,000 and 20,000 respectively, each accompanied by a certificate. The total prize pool was 2,00,000, including₹ ₹ ₹ ₹  
overall cash awards, track-wise prizes and goodies. This report records the competition format, track themes, results, partner  
categories, documented impact and recommendations for future editions.

2. Introduction
Student hackathons provide a focused environment in which teams can turn an initial idea into a proposed or working technical  
solution. VIT Code Apex 3.0 used a  staged competition model to give participants a  path from proposal screening to live  
presentation and time-constrained implementation. The event emphasized technical creativity, problem understanding, feasibility  
and the ability to communicate a solution.
Organized by AISF at VIT Pune, Code Apex 3.0 brought together a large registration pool and teams from multiple colleges. The  
four-track  design  combined  industry-defined  problem  statements  with  an  open-innovation  option.  This  helped  accommodate 
participants interested in applied AI, software engineering, cloud systems, cybersecurity, data science, IoT, blockchain/Web3 and  
related emerging technologies.

3. Objectives
3.1 Encourage Practical Problem-Solving
The multi-stage format was designed to move participants from explaining a concept to presenting a reasoned solution and then  
attempting implementation during the finale. The final stage gave selected teams a defined period to develop and demonstrate their  
proposed work.
3.2 Promote Technical Innovation
The event’s broad technology focus and specialized tracks created opportunities to apply software and emerging technologies to  
industrial  and  social-impact  problems.  The  named  challenge  themes  emphasized  practical  use  cases  rather  than  a  single  
programming language or technology stack.
3.3 Connect Students with Industry Challenges
The Emerson and iMocha tracks presented named industry-associated problem themes, while the Technology for Social Impact  
track was powered by UST. The Open Innovation track allowed participants to frame their own problem and solution. These  
formats offered different ways for students to engage with industry-relevant and self-defined challenges.
3.4 Develop Collaboration and Communication
A team-based hackathon requires participants to divide work, coordinate implementation and communicate decisions. Online jury  
pitching and final demonstrations placed presentation and explanation alongside technical work as visible parts of the competition.
3.5 Recognize Student Effort and Achievement
Overall awards and certificates recognized the top three teams. The stated prize pool also included track-wise awards and goodies.  
Track-wise winner names are not listed in this report because verified names were not present in the supplied final-report material.
3.6 Build a Multi-College Innovation Community
Participation from 125 colleges and the progression of selected teams through successive rounds gave the event a broad inter-
college scope. The event also brought together the organizing body, partner organizations and participants around a common  
technology-focused activity.

6.1 Track 1 – Emerson
The Emerson-associated track included three named challenge themes. These addressed industrial process documentation, I/O  
allocation and control-cabinet inspection, using AI-oriented approaches.
Project UNTANGLE
Recorded theme: AI-based conversion of Piping and Instrumentation Diagram (P&ID) diagrams into simplified process sketches.  
The challenge focused on making information represented in technical diagrams easier to interpret in a simplified process view.
Project SIGNAL SUDOKU
Recorded theme: AI-assisted DeltaV I/O allocation and rule-based optimization. The challenge focused on assisting allocation  
decisions within an industrial control context.
Project EAGLE EYE
Recorded theme: AI vision-based quality inspection of control cabinets. This theme applied visual analysis to quality inspection.
The report retains Emerson as the industry partner associated with Track 1. No additional financial, mentoring or technical  
contribution is attributed without supporting documentation.

6.2 Track 2 – iMocha
The iMocha-associated track listed five challenge themes related to AI-assisted coding, software quality assurance, skills evidence,  
workplace simulation and codebase understanding. The summaries below follow the theme names and descriptions in the existing  
3.0 report.
Vibe Coding
Recorded theme: AI-era coding assessment involving AI-assisted development, candidate-journey tracking and skills reporting.  
The emphasis is on assessment in a workflow where AI tools may be used as part of development, rather than on code output alone.
Autonomous AI QA Engineer
Recorded theme: an agent that explores web applications, generates and runs tests, and reports bugs with evidence. The theme  
combines application exploration, test execution and evidence-backed defect reporting.
Skill Passport
Recorded  theme:  an  AI-powered  verified  skill  profile  built  from  real  work,  with  evidence-based  skills,  role  matching  and 
personalized learning paths. The focus is on linking skill claims to evidence and using that evidence to support role alignment and  
learning recommendations.
AI Job Simulator
Recorded theme: workplace simulation and evidence-based feedback.
Codebase Mentor
Recorded theme: AI assistance for understanding unfamiliar codebases.
These are the challenge themes recorded in the 2026 report. No team-to-challenge mapping or implementation outcome is asserted

A sequence of online screening, live jury pitches and an on-campus finale provides a way to review a large registration pool before  
allocating the intensive final-stage opportunity. For future editions, the organizer can retain stage-by-stage counts and exact  
submission totals so the participation funnel can be reported precisely.

retaining a canonical problem statement for each challenge, including scope, expected deliverables, constraints and the judging  
rubric approved by the track owner.
12.3 Transparent Evaluation Records
Publishing a clear rubric to participants and preserving a signed result record can make the process easier to explain and audit.
12.4 Operational Documentation
A 24-hour on-campus event benefits from a single schedule and documented roles. For future editions, AISF should retain venue  
and  technical  checklists,  volunteer  assignments,  contact  information,  issue  logs  and  a  post-event  closeout  note.  These  
recommendations do not imply that any particular facility or incident was missing during the event itself.

complete  approved  award  sheet  would  make  it  easier  to  distinguish  branding,  track  ownership,  prize  support  and  other  
contributions without inference.

12. Key Learnings and Recommendations
12.1 Multi-Stage Screening
A sequence of online screening, live jury pitches and an on-campus finale provides a way to review a large registration pool before  
allocating the intensive final-stage opportunity. For future editions, the organizer can retain stage-by-stage counts and exact  
submission totals so the participation funnel can be reported precisely.
12.2 Clarity of Challenge Statements
The event used both named industry challenges and an open-innovation track. Future documentation can strengthen consistency by  
retaining a canonical problem statement for each challenge, including scope, expected deliverables, constraints and the judging  
rubric approved by the track owner.
12.3 Transparent Evaluation Records
Publishing a clear rubric to participants and preserving a signed result record can make the process easier to explain and audit.
12.4 Operational Documentation
A 24-hour on-campus event benefits from a single schedule and documented roles. For future editions, AISF should retain venue  
and  technical  checklists,  volunteer  assignments,  contact  information,  issue  logs  and  a  post-event  closeout  note.  These  
recommendations do not imply that any particular facility or incident was missing during the event itself.
12.5 Partner and Award Records
Sponsor categories, industry associations and overall awards are recorded in this report. A partner-contribution matrix and a  
complete  approved  award  sheet  would  make  it  easier  to  distinguish  branding,  track  ownership,  prize  support  and  other  
contributions without inference.
12.6 Future-Edition Improvement Checklist
 Record exact registrations and completed submissions separately.
 Retain the dated shortlist for each round and final result approval.
 Archive jury names, affiliations, evaluation rubrics and score sheets.
 Store the final event run sheet and confirmed participant-support details.
 Collect optional participant feedback with a documented method and response count.
 Maintain approved sponsor contribution descriptions and award-distribution evidence.
